# Turn a halo exchange into a byte rate

[Count the bytes before timing them, and keep the denominator honest.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

The [halo-frames lesson](../halo-frames/index.qmd) records every exchange as
a profiling frame. This chapter asks a narrower question with the
`25_halo_bandwidth` program: for a cubic grid of side $N$, how many bytes
does each exchange send to other ranks, and at what rate? The program
allocates a padded field and exchanges its halo repeatedly. It steps no
model, and the field values play no part in the result.

The default exchange uses only the $\pm x$ faces. `--axis y` or `--axis z`
selects another pair, and `--faces` uses all six. The host facade is the
default; a CUDA or HIP build also accepts `--cuda` or `--hip`.

## Count the bytes before timing them

Each rank owns a brick of $n_x\times n_y\times n_z$ cells. With a process
grid $g_x\times g_y\times g_z$ that divides the grid, $n_a=N/g_a$. A face
normal to axis $a$ with halo width $h$ holds $h$ layers of the other two
owned dimensions, in double precision:

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="bytes"}
```

$$
B_x=8h\,n_y n_z,\qquad B_y=8h\,n_x n_z,\qquad B_z=8h\,n_x n_y .
$$

Not every face crosses a rank boundary. The domain is periodic in every
axis, so on an undivided axis ($g_a=1$) both faces wrap around to the same
rank. The program classifies each selected face by its neighbor:

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="peers" dedent=4}
```

A self face is still exchanged; the host exchanger posts it as an MPI
message from the rank to itself. It crosses no rank boundary, so it does not
count in `Send_B`.

Two ranks on a cube get the automatic grid $1\times1\times2$: the split is
along $z$. For $N=64$ each rank owns a $64\times64\times32$ brick. Its
$\pm z$ faces both go to the other rank. With two ranks on a periodic axis,
the neighbor in $+z$ is also the neighbor in $-z$:

$$
\mathtt{Send\_B}=2B_z=2\cdot 8\cdot 64\cdot 64=65\,536 \text{ bytes}.
$$

On the same grid the default $\pm x$ pair and `--axis y` select self faces
only. `Send_B` is zero, so the rate is zero, yet the exchange still takes
time. `--faces` sends the two $z$ faces and adds four self faces. The table
reports these counts in `RemoteFaces`, `SelfFaces` and `OffNodeFaces`, the
last being remote faces whose peer runs on another host. Read the `grid`
in the header before reading any rate. `OPENPFC_FD_PROC_GRID=gx,gy,gz`
selects another split when it divides the grid.

## Time the exchange alone

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="timing" dedent=2}
```

Warmup exchanges run before the clock starts. A barrier then aligns the
ranks, and the program averages $K$ exchanges between two barriers:

$$
t_r=\frac{t^{\mathrm{end}}_r-t^{\mathrm{start}}_r}{K}.
$$

The interval includes the wait at the trailing barrier. It excludes field
allocation, decomposition and the construction of the exchanger.

## Divide by the slowest rank

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="rate" dedent=2}
```

The table combines the busiest sender with the slowest rank:

$$
\mathtt{Uni\_GBps}=\frac{\max_r \mathtt{Send\_B}_r}{10^9\,\max_r t_r},
\qquad
\mathtt{Duplex\_GBps}=2\,\mathtt{Uni\_GBps}.
$$

One GB here is $10^9$ bytes. The duplex column assumes that every rank
receives as much as it sends, which holds for the divisible, periodic
splits used in this chapter. If ranks send different amounts, the row
adds `send_min`.

This rate is not a link bandwidth. Its time also contains packing and
unpacking, the self-face messages, the trailing barrier and, on a
device, any staging through host memory. The header records whether the
exchanger uses GPU-aware MPI. Compare rows from the same machine,
placement and build, and read small sizes as latency rather than
throughput.

## Run a small host experiment

With a matching installed CPU SDK, compile the [complete model](model.cpp)
and run it on two ranks:

```sh
openpfc compile model.cpp -o halo-bandwidth
mkdir -p results/halo-bandwidth
cd results/halo-bandwidth
mpirun -n 2 ../../halo-bandwidth --axis z --sizes 64,128,256
```

One run on a single Tohtori CPU node printed:

```text
# OpenPFC halo bandwidth
# backend host device host
# ranks 2 nodes 1 grid 1x1x2 directions z halo 1 iters 50 warmup 5
# gpu_aware n/a
# rank_device 0:-1 1:-1
# Uni_GBps = remote send bytes / time / 1e9; Duplex_GBps = 2 * Uni_GBps
# N Send_B Time_us Uni_GBps Duplex_GBps RemoteFaces SelfFaces OffNodeFaces
64 65536 31.1 2.104 4.209 2 0 0
128 262144 37.5 6.996 13.992 2 0 0
256 1048576 154.8 6.775 13.551 2 0 0
```

The `Send_B` column follows from the grid alone: $2\cdot8N^2$ bytes. The
times and rates belong to this machine, placement and moment, and another
run will differ. At $N=64$ the time hardly changes from $N=128$ although the
bytes quadruple; such small messages measure latency more than throughput.

The built checkout target keeps the name `25_halo_bandwidth`. Build it
through `scripts/build.sh` and find it under the build's `examples/`
directory. GPU variants need the corresponding build and a scheduler
allocation with one device per rank.

Before running more cases, predict `Send_B` and the face counts for each:

- the default $\pm x$ pair and `--axis y` on the automatic two-rank grid;
- `OPENPFC_FD_PROC_GRID=2,1,1` with the default $\pm x$ pair, where each
  exchanged face is a $y$–$z$ plane, strided in the $x$-fastest field rather
  than contiguous like the $x$–$y$ planes of a $z$ split;
- `--faces --halo 2`.

The checker runs the automatic $z$ split and four cases with a selected
grid: $\pm x$ and $\pm y$ on $2\times1\times1$, $\pm z$ on $1\times1\times2$,
and all faces with $h=2$ on $2\times1\times1$, each at $N=16$ and $32$. It
recomputes every byte count and face class from the printed grid. It also
checks that the two rate columns agree with `Send_B` and the time to their
printed precision. It imposes no speed threshold.

:::
